prompt:
Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit.

We represent: plaintiff employee.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that an employer that fails to engage in the interactive process is liable under the ADA when that failure prevents identification of a reasonable accommodation.

Cite at least six decisions of the Seventh Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.

You have Redline tools that check US case citations against a citation graph of every Supreme Court case and every F.3d appeals case. Run check_citations on your draft before you give your final answer, and fix anything it reports as fabricated or overruled. Use search_cases and get_case to look authorities up.
answer:
**ARGUMENT**

**I. An employer that fails to engage in the interactive process is liable under the ADA when that failure prevents identification of a reasonable accommodation.**

The ADA defines discrimination to include "not making reasonable accommodations to the known physical or mental limitations of an otherwise qualified individual." 42 U.S.C. § 12112(b)(5)(A). The regulations contemplate an "informal, interactive process" to identify the limitation and the accommodations that could overcome it. 29 C.F.R. § 1630.2(o)(3). This Court has treated that process as the mechanism through which the statutory duty is carried out. *Beck v. Univ. of Wis. Bd. of Regents*, 75 F.3d 1130, 1135 (7th Cir. 1996). An employer that stops short of that process cannot say that no accommodation was available when its own conduct kept one from being found.

**A. Both parties must participate in good faith, and the employer cannot avoid its share.**

Once an employee makes the employer aware of a disability and a need for accommodation, the employer must engage in a flexible, good-faith dialogue. *Beck*, 75 F.3d at 1135; *Bultemeyer v. Fort Wayne Cmty. Schs.*, 100 F.3d 1281, 1285 (7th Cir. 1996). The employer may not wait for the employee to name the perfect accommodation. In *Bultemeyer*, the employee's mental illness made it hard for him to articulate what he needed. This Court held that the employer had to take the lead by asking for more information and exploring options. *Id.* at 1285. An employer that meets a request with silence, or with a rigid refusal, has not met that obligation. *See Hansen v. Henderson*, 233 F.3d 521, 523 (7th Cir. 2000).

**B. Liability attaches when the employer is responsible for the breakdown.**

Where the process fails, the question is who caused the failure. *Beck* held that an employer cannot be held liable if the employee was the one who caused the breakdown. It follows that an employer who caused the breakdown can be held liable. 75 F.3d at 1135–36; *see also Rehling v. City of Chicago*, 207 F.3d 1009, 1015–16 (7th Cir. 2000). In *EEOC v. Sears, Roebuck & Co.*, this Court affirmed liability against an employer that did not engage in good faith. It held that an employer who fails to engage "is liable" when the process would have led to a reasonable accommodation, and that the employer could not prevail by pointing to the absence of an accommodation that its own inaction kept the parties from identifying. 417 F.3d 789, 805–07 (7th Cir. 2005). *Ozlowski v. Henderson* applies the same principle: an employer that does not engage in good faith when notified of an employee's need cannot defeat the claim by pointing to the lack of a proposed accommodation. 237 F.3d 837, 840 (7th Cir. 2001).

**C. The causation requirement is met when the failure prevented identification of an accommodation.**

The failure to engage is not a freestanding violation. The employee must show that the failure prevented identification of an appropriate accommodation for a qualified individual. *Rehling*, 207 F.3d at 1015–16; *Jackson v. City of Chicago*, 414 F.3d 806, 813 (7th Cir. 2005); *Basden v. Prof'l Transp., Inc.*, 714 F.3d 1034, 1037–38 (7th Cir. 2013). That showing is met here. [Plaintiff] told [Employer] of [his/her] limitations and asked for relief. [Employer] did not request medical information, discuss alternatives, or propose any option. Had it done so, the dialogue would have identified accommodations such as [reassignment, modified schedule, or equipment]. These were available and would not have imposed an undue hardship. *Cf. Sears*, 417 F.3d at 806–07. The record shows that no accommodation was identified because [Employer] never took part in the process. It does not show that none existed.

Requiring the employee to prove a specific accommodation that the employer's refusal to talk kept from surfacing would reward the very conduct the interactive process exists to prevent. *See Bultemeyer*, 100 F.3d at 1285; *Gile v. United Airlines, Inc.*, 95 F.3d 492, 499 (7th Cir. 1996). A plaintiff meets the burden by showing that a reasonable accommodation was possible, and this Court's cases do not require more. The district court's contrary conclusion should be reversed.
